This seems to tie back to the paper Adaptive Auto-Harness: Sustained Self-Improvement for Agentic System Deployment on Open-Ended Task Streams[0].

In the Emory paper:

    > We reduce this loss by expanding Φ with a stateful four-phase multi-agent evolver, temporal-reveal feedback, and cross-cycle memory. This design targets the unbounded-stream failure where a single-agent evolver must absorb growing trajectories, delayed labels, and prior research within one context window
TL;DR: the solution approach uses "multi-agent evolution" and "multi-agent with distinct roles and objectives" for "solve-time adaptation" and improves performance with streams of heterogeneous tasks. The Emory team overall has congruent findings:

    > The experiments further show that...multi-agent evolution constructs benchmark-specific capabilities
Intuitively, the reason this works seems to be simple: multiple agents results in context spread to each agent by specific role. Each agent role only outputs the final, relevant result and not the noisy thinking tokens, tool calls, etc. so subsequent agents get smaller, more focused context, auto-adapting to each new task with prompt refinement at each step as the solution approach emerges.

So far, the comments have focused on hopes for the effectiveness of open-weight models versus proprietary frontier models. That's fine, but I'm thinking about the approach and the results, as opposed to the model.

Taking the results at face value, what is it about the "team" that makes the system so effective? That's the key here: presumably, the approach should work regardless of the model, open-weight or otherwise.

My guess would be that the division of labor makes the separate contexts more effective. This is an optimization around the limits of context. Some of that is simply the net amount of context brought to bear: each team member has a context, so the net amount of context is multiplied by the number of team members. Also, since the division limits the scope of each team member's focus, the context a team member has is used more effectively.
